options: Cephalic vein
Median cubital vein
Basilic vein
Brachial vein

why.correct: The median cubital vein (cubit- = elbow) crosses the front of the elbow diagonally between the cephalic and basilic veins. It is the usual site for drawing blood.
options: The cephalic vein runs up the thumb side of the forearm and the outer arm. It is one of the two veins the pinned vein connects.
Correct. The median cubital vein links the cephalic and basilic veins in front of the elbow.
The basilic vein runs up the little-finger side and the inner arm. It is the other vein the pinned vein connects.
The brachial veins are deep veins that run beside the brachial artery. They are not visible under the skin.
Femoral vein
Small saphenous vein
Popliteal vein
Great saphenous vein

why.correct: The great saphenous vein starts at the inner end of the dorsal venous arch and joins the femoral vein just below the groin. It is the longest vein in the body.
options: The femoral vein is a deep vein that runs beside the femoral artery. The great saphenous vein drains into it at the groin.
The small saphenous vein runs up the back of the calf from behind the outer ankle and ends at the knee.
The popliteal vein is a deep vein behind the knee. It does not run up the inner side of the thigh.
Correct. The great saphenous vein runs the length of the inner leg.
Superior sagittal sinus
Transverse sinus
Sigmoid sinus
Cavernous sinus

why.correct: The superior sagittal sinus runs along the top midline in the fold of dura between the two cerebral hemispheres. Cerebrospinal fluid drains into it through the arachnoid granulations.
options: Correct. It runs front to back along the top of the skull.
The transverse sinuses run sideways around the back of the skull, receiving blood from the superior sagittal sinus.
The sigmoid sinuses are the S-shaped channels at the base of the skull that become the internal jugular veins.
The cavernous sinuses sit on each side of the sphenoid bone, deep in the skull base, not along the top.
Inferior vena cava
Superior mesenteric vein
Hepatic portal vein
Splenic vein

why.correct: The hepatic portal vein forms behind the pancreas where the superior mesenteric and splenic veins join. It carries blood from the gut's capillaries to the liver's sinusoids.
options: The inferior vena cava receives blood from the liver through the hepatic veins, after the liver has processed it. No gut vein drains into it directly.
The superior mesenteric vein is a tributary of the pinned vein. It drains most of the intestines, while the pinned vessel collects from the stomach, spleen and pancreas as well.
Correct. The hepatic portal vein collects blood from all the gut organs and delivers it to the liver.
The splenic vein is the other main tributary. It drains the spleen and parts of the pancreas and stomach.
Brachiocephalic vein
Superior vena cava
Azygos vein
External jugular vein

why.correct: Behind each sternoclavicular joint, the internal jugular and subclavian veins join to form a brachiocephalic vein. The right and left brachiocephalic veins then join to form the superior vena cava.
options: Correct. There are two brachiocephalic veins, unlike the single brachiocephalic trunk on the arterial side.
The superior vena cava is formed one step later, where the two brachiocephalic veins meet.
The azygos vein drains the chest wall and joins the back of the superior vena cava.
The external jugular vein is a superficial neck vein that drains into the subclavian vein.

q: Put the channels in order to trace blood from the top of the brain back to the heart.
options: Superior sagittal sinus
Transverse sinus
Sigmoid sinus
Internal jugular vein
Brachiocephalic vein
Superior vena cava

why.correct: Blood in the superior sagittal sinus runs to the back of the skull, turns sideways into a transverse sinus, curves down as the sigmoid sinus and leaves the skull as the internal jugular vein. That joins the subclavian vein as the brachiocephalic vein, and the two brachiocephalic veins form the superior vena cava.

q: A glucose molecule is absorbed into a capillary in the wall of the intestine. Put its route to the right atrium in order.
options: Superior mesenteric vein
Hepatic portal vein
Sinusoids of the liver
Hepatic veins
Inferior vena cava
Right atrium

why.correct: Intestinal capillaries drain into the superior mesenteric vein, which joins the splenic vein to form the hepatic portal vein. That vein branches to the liver's sinusoids, the second capillary bed. The sinusoids drain into the hepatic veins, which empty into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.

q: A drug is 90% broken down by the liver on its first pass. A patient receives the same dose once as a pill and once by IV into an arm vein. Why does far less of the swallowed dose reach the rest of the body?
options: Gut blood passes through the liver first
The stomach's acid destroys most drugs before absorption
Arm veins deliver drug straight to the liver
Swallowed drug enters the inferior vena cava first

why.correct: Blood from the gut goes through the hepatic portal vein to the liver's sinusoids before it can reach the heart. The liver breaks down much of the drug on this first pass. IV drug in an arm vein goes to the heart and out to the body without passing through the liver first.
options: Correct. The hepatic portal system routes everything absorbed from the gut through the liver first.
Stomach acid does break down some drugs, but the question states that the liver removes most of this one. Acid alone does not explain a 90% loss.
Arm veins drain through the subclavian and brachiocephalic veins to the superior vena cava and the heart. They do not lead to the liver.
Gut veins do not drain into the inferior vena cava directly. Blood reaches it only after passing through the liver.

q: Fill the gap in the deep veins of the leg: posterior tibial vein → ____ → femoral vein → external iliac vein.
options: Great saphenous vein
Popliteal vein
Common iliac vein
Deep femoral vein

why.correct: The tibial and fibular veins of the calf join behind the knee as the popliteal vein, which continues up the thigh as the femoral vein.
options: The great saphenous vein is superficial. It joins the femoral vein near the groin but is not part of the deep chain from the calf.
Correct. The popliteal vein links the calf veins to the femoral vein.
The common iliac vein comes after the external iliac vein, higher up in the pelvis.
The deep femoral vein drains the thigh muscles into the femoral vein. It does not carry blood from the calf.

q: Select every vein that is superficial, running under the skin with no artery beside it.
options: Cephalic vein
Femoral vein
Basilic vein
Great saphenous vein
Popliteal vein
External jugular vein

why.correct: The cephalic, basilic, great saphenous and external jugular veins run in the fat under the skin and have their own names. Deep veins such as the femoral and popliteal veins run beside arteries of the same name.
options: Correct. The cephalic vein runs up the thumb side of the arm under the skin.
The femoral vein is a deep vein beside the femoral artery.
Correct. The basilic vein runs up the inner forearm and arm under the skin before diving deep.
Correct. The great saphenous vein runs up the inner leg under the skin.
The popliteal vein is a deep vein behind the knee, beside the popliteal artery.
Correct. The external jugular vein runs across the side of the neck just under the skin.

q: Why is the left brachiocephalic vein longer than the right one?
options: It drains the left arm, which is supplied by a longer artery
It crosses the midline to reach the superior vena cava
It also collects blood returning from the heart muscle
The aortic arch pushes it upward and outward into the neck

why.correct: The superior vena cava sits on the right side, entering the right atrium. The left brachiocephalic vein has to cross in front of the arch's branches to reach it, so it is about two to three times as long as the right one.
options: The left arm's artery does arise differently, straight from the arch, but vein length is set by the route back to the heart, and the two arms drain the same way.
Correct. Crossing the midline makes the left vein longer.
The heart muscle drains mainly through the coronary sinus into the right atrium, not through the brachiocephalic veins.
The left brachiocephalic vein runs across the upper chest in front of the arch's branches. Its length comes from the distance to the right side, not from being pushed upward.

q: A teenager squeezes an infected pimple beside his nose. Days later he has a high temperature, a swollen eye and double vision. Which structure has the infection most likely reached?
options: Superior sagittal sinus
External jugular vein
Cavernous sinus
Great saphenous vein

why.correct: Veins around the nose and upper lip connect with the cavernous sinus beside the sphenoid bone, and blood in them can flow toward the skull. Nerves to the eye muscles pass through or beside the cavernous sinus, so infection there causes eye swelling and double vision.
options: The superior sagittal sinus runs along the top of the skull. It is not directly connected to the face veins near the nose, and it is not beside the nerves to the eye muscles.
The external jugular vein drains the scalp and side of the face down into the neck, away from the skull.
Correct. Face veins near the nose link to the cavernous sinus.
The great saphenous vein is in the leg and has no connection to the face.

q: Which vessels carry blood out of the liver?
options: Hepatic portal vein
Hepatic veins
Superior mesenteric vein
Splenic vein

why.correct: The hepatic veins collect blood from the liver's sinusoids and drain into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.
options: The hepatic portal vein carries blood into the liver, from the gut.
Correct. The hepatic veins are the liver's exits.
The superior mesenteric vein drains the intestines into the hepatic portal vein. It carries blood toward the liver.
The splenic vein drains the spleen into the hepatic portal vein. It also carries blood toward the liver.

q: A student traced blood from the back of the right hand to the heart along the superficial route. Which step is wrong?
options: Veins on the back of the hand drain into the cephalic vein on the thumb side
The cephalic vein drains into the axillary vein
The axillary vein continues as the subclavian vein
The subclavian vein drains straight into the superior vena cava
The superior vena cava empties into the right atrium

why.correct: The subclavian vein first joins the internal jugular vein to form the right brachiocephalic vein. Only then do the right and left brachiocephalic veins form the superior vena cava.
options: This step is right. The cephalic vein starts from the network on the back of the hand, on the thumb side.
This step is right. The cephalic vein runs up the outer arm and drains into the axillary vein near the shoulder.
This step is right. The axillary vein is renamed subclavian at the outer edge of the first rib.
This is the error. A brachiocephalic vein sits between the subclavian vein and the superior vena cava.
This step is right. The superior vena cava enters the top of the right atrium.

q: Years of heavy drinking have scarred a man's liver, so blood flows through it with difficulty. He vomits a large amount of blood. Which explanation fits the hepatic portal system?
options: Portal blood detours through esophageal veins, which burst
The hepatic veins block, and blood backs up into the aorta
The arteries to the stomach close, and its wall breaks down
Scarring stops the hepatic portal vein from forming at all

why.correct: A scarred liver resists flow, so pressure rises in the hepatic portal vein and its tributaries. Blood takes detours through small connections to systemic veins, including those at the lower end of the esophagus. These veins swell and can rupture, causing heavy bleeding.
options: Correct. Backed-up portal blood reroutes through thin-walled veins that can bleed.
Veins do not drain into the aorta. Backed-up venous blood cannot reach an artery, and the liver scarring affects flow through the sinusoids, not the aorta.
Liver scarring affects the venous side, not the arteries to the stomach, and a dead stomach wall would not explain sudden heavy bleeding.
The portal vein forms behind the pancreas, outside the liver. Liver scarring does not stop it from forming; it raises the pressure inside it.

q: How does a dural venous sinus differ from an ordinary vein?
options: It carries oxygenated blood
No smooth muscle or valves; dura holds it open
It has a thicker tunica media than any artery
It carries cerebrospinal fluid instead of blood

why.correct: A dural sinus is a channel between the two layers of the dura mater, lined by endothelium. Its wall has no smooth muscle and it has no valves; the stiff dura keeps it open.
options: Dural sinuses carry deoxygenated blood from the brain, like other systemic veins.
Correct. Its wall is dura, not a three-layered vessel wall.
A dural sinus has no tunica media at all. Its wall is made of dura.
Cerebrospinal fluid drains into the superior sagittal sinus and mixes with the blood there, but the sinuses carry venous blood.

q: A paramedic is examining a stabbing victim sitting up at 45 degrees. The veins on both sides of his neck, just under the skin, are full and bulging. Which vein is she looking at, and what does its filling suggest?
options: The external jugular vein; pressure in the right atrium is high
The internal jugular vein; blood flow to the brain is blocked by the wound
The carotid artery; the heart is pumping harder
The vertebral vein; the neck vertebrae are injured

why.correct: The external jugular vein runs just under the skin of the neck and drains through the subclavian and brachiocephalic veins to the superior vena cava. At 45 degrees it is normally flat. If it stays full, blood is backing up because pressure in the right atrium is high, as when blood around the heart squeezes it in cardiac tamponade.
options: Correct. A bulging external jugular vein reflects high pressure where the veins empty into the heart.
The internal jugular vein is deep, under a neck muscle, and it carries blood away from the brain, not to it.
The carotid artery is deep and pulses; it does not bulge as a full, soft vein.
The vertebral veins run inside the holes of the neck vertebrae and cannot be seen.
